title: Enteral Tube Placement: Verify Before Feeding
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Do not start feeding or give medication through a newly placed or questionably positioned tube until placement is verified by the method required for that device and setting. New coughing, respiratory distress, unexplained desaturation, or tube-length change requires reassessment.
recognize: External tube-length change, new coughing, respiratory symptoms, or inability to aspirate as expected can indicate displacement.
Bedside checks do not replace the facility's required initial-placement verification process.
priorities: Stop feeding when displacement is suspected.
Verify placement according to device, order, and facility policy before use.
assessMonitor: Track tube position markings, respiratory status, abdominal symptoms, and feeding tolerance.
interventions: Secure tubing and minimize accidental traction.
medicationSafety: Never give medication through a tube whose position is uncertain.
redFlags: Acute coughing or dyspnea during feeding
teaching: Patients/caregivers should stop home feeds and call for guidance if the tube appears displaced or breathing changes occur.
delegationScope: Tube-use authority and placement verification vary by device and setting; follow facility policy and state scope.
examTrap: Using a tube because it flushed easily even though its position changed.
oneLinePearl: Easy flush does not prove correct placement.

title: Enteral Feeding Aspiration: Position and Tolerance Matter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Aspiration risk rises with impaired consciousness, dysphagia, vomiting, poor gastric emptying, and improper positioning. Protect the airway and reassess feeding when respiratory or GI tolerance worsens.
recognize: Coughing, wet voice, vomiting, rising oxygen need, tachypnea, or new crackles during feeding are concerning.
Silent aspiration can occur without dramatic coughing.
priorities: Keep the patient positioned according to feeding protocol and condition.
Stop the feed and escalate with new respiratory deterioration or repeated emesis.
assessMonitor: Monitor respiratory status, level of consciousness, nausea/vomiting, abdominal distention, bowel function, and ordered tolerance parameters.
interventions: Maintain prescribed head elevation and oral care.
medicationSafety: Sedatives and drugs that impair motility can increase aspiration risk and should be considered during medication review.
teaching: Follow positioning instructions during and after home feeds and report recurrent coughing or breathing changes.
delegationScope: Routine positioning may be delegated; interpretation of intolerance and respiratory decline requires licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Continuing a feed because gastric residual information alone appears acceptable despite worsening respiratory status.
oneLinePearl: Tolerance is clinical, not one number.
sourceBasis: CDC aspiration-prevention principles for enteral feeding

title: Interrupted Tube Feeds: Protect Fluids, Glucose, and Medication Timing
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: An interrupted feed can change hydration, glucose exposure, and medication timing. When feeds stop unexpectedly, identify why and review the patient's insulin, fluid, and medication plan rather than simply restarting later.
recognize: Pump alarms, procedures, vomiting, tube occlusion, or disconnection may interrupt nutrition.
Patients receiving insulin may become hypoglycemic when carbohydrate delivery stops.
priorities: Identify the cause of interruption and assess glucose/clinical status when relevant.
Coordinate restart and medication adjustments with the prescribed plan.
assessMonitor: Track feed volume delivered, glucose, hydration, and medication timing.
interventions: Document interruptions accurately and communicate prolonged deficits.
medicationSafety: Never continue scheduled nutritional insulin blindly when carbohydrate delivery has stopped; use the ordered contingency plan and escalate if unclear.
teaching: Home patients need a written plan for pump failure, feed interruption, and glucose checks when applicable.
delegationScope: Medication changes require prescriber/protocol authority; PN/LVN role is recognition, ordered implementation, and escalation.
examTrap: Treating the feeding pump and insulin schedule as unrelated systems.
oneLinePearl: If nutrition stops, reassess everything tied to nutrition.

title: Refeeding Risk: Nutrition Can Shift Electrolytes Fast
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Severely malnourished patients can develop dangerous electrolyte and fluid shifts when nutrition is restarted. Phosphate, potassium, magnesium, glucose, fluid balance, and cardiopulmonary status require close monitoring during early refeeding.
recognize: Profound weight loss, prolonged minimal intake, alcoholism, cancer, eating disorders, and severe chronic illness increase risk.
Weakness, edema, arrhythmia, respiratory decline, or neurologic change after feeding begins can reflect electrolyte shifts.
priorities: Identify high-risk patients before aggressive nutrition advancement.
Escalate new arrhythmia, respiratory weakness, severe edema, or major electrolyte abnormality.
assessMonitor: Trend phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, glucose, weight, edema, respiratory status, and cardiac symptoms as ordered.
interventions: Advance nutrition according to the prescribed refeeding plan rather than rapidly replacing the full estimated requirement.
medicationSafety: Electrolyte replacement is dose- and route-specific; IV replacement authority varies by setting.
teaching: Patients with prolonged poor intake should not self-correct with abrupt very-high-calorie intake when medically fragile.
delegationScope: Nutrition advancement and electrolyte replacement require ordered plans; PN/LVN monitors and escalates abnormalities.
examTrap: Assuming more calories are always safer when severe malnutrition is present.
oneLinePearl: Starvation adapts slowly; refeeding must respect that adaptation.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. clinical nutrition safety principles

title: Parenteral Nutrition Line Safety: Treat the Line as High Risk
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Parenteral nutrition is a high-risk infusion delivered through vascular access. Line contamination, misconnections, precipitation, thrombosis, and catheter problems can become serious quickly.
recognize: Fever, chills, line pain, drainage, pump alarms, leakage, resistance, or unexplained metabolic change require attention.
Central parenteral nutrition requires meticulous catheter and tubing management.
priorities: Use strict aseptic technique and trace the line from bag to patient.
Stop and escalate if the line leaks, disconnects, or the solution appears abnormal.
assessMonitor: Monitor line site, temperature, pump function, infusion rate, glucose, electrolytes, fluid balance, and ordered labs.
interventions: Follow product/facility filtration, tubing-change, and dedicated-lumen requirements.
medicationSafety: Do not add medications to PN or co-infuse through the same lumen without explicit compatibility and pharmacy guidance.
teaching: Home PN patients should know sterile connection technique and when to stop the pump and call for help.
delegationScope: Central-line and PN responsibilities vary by state/facility competency; verify scope.
examTrap: Treating PN as just another bag of IV fluid.
oneLinePearl: PN is nutrition delivered through a high-risk vascular device.
sourceBasis: FDA parenteral-nutrition labeling and infusion-pump safety principles

title: Parenteral Nutrition Monitoring: Glucose and Electrolytes Can Move Quickly
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Parenteral nutrition can rapidly change glucose, fluid, and electrolyte balance. Monitor trends and avoid abrupt, unplanned changes to a high-dextrose infusion.
recognize: Hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia after interruption, electrolyte shifts, fluid overload, and liver abnormalities can occur.
priorities: Track ordered glucose and laboratory monitoring.
Escalate symptomatic glucose disturbance, major electrolyte change, or fluid overload.
assessMonitor: Monitor glucose, electrolytes, weight, intake/output, edema, liver tests, triglycerides when ordered, and clinical tolerance.
interventions: Use the ordered contingency plan for unplanned interruption or pump failure.
medicationSafety: Insulin may be linked to PN delivery; interruption requires coordinated glucose management.
teaching: Home PN patients need a clear backup plan for pump or power failure.
delegationScope: PN formulation/insulin decisions remain prescriber/pharmacy responsibilities; PN/LVN monitors and escalates.
examTrap: Stopping a high-dextrose infusion without considering glucose consequences.
oneLinePearl: PN changes metabolism as well as calories.

title: Feeding-Tube Clogs: Prevent Before You Push
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Tube clogs are easier to prevent than to clear. Use ordered flushing practices, correct medication preparation, and avoid force that could rupture or displace the tube.
recognize: Increasing resistance or inability to flush suggests occlusion; sudden pain or leakage can indicate a device problem rather than a simple clog.
priorities: Stop forcing fluid when resistance is significant.
Use the facility-approved unclogging approach and escalate persistent occlusion.
assessMonitor: Review flush schedule, medications, feed viscosity, tube type, and recent resistance.
interventions: Flush before/after medications and between medications according to protocol when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not crush medications that must remain intact or mix multiple medications together in the tube.
teaching: Home caregivers should never use excessive pressure or unapproved chemicals to clear a tube.
delegationScope: Unclogging procedures and device replacement vary by role and facility.
examTrap: Using more force because the tube is hard to flush.
oneLinePearl: Resistance is a warning, not an invitation to push harder.

title: Medications Through Feeding Tubes: Formulation Rules Still Apply
bottomLine: A feeding tube changes the route, not the medication's formulation rules. Verify whether each drug can be crushed, opened, diluted, separated from feeds, or requires another formulation.
recognize: Extended-release, enteric-coated, hazardous, sublingual/buccal, or specially formulated drugs may be unsafe to crush.
priorities: Verify formulation and tube location before administration.
Separate medications and flush according to protocol.
assessMonitor: Monitor therapeutic response, tube patency, and feed-drug interaction concerns.
interventions: Consult pharmacy for uncertain formulations or feed interactions.
medicationSafety: Do not mix all medications together or add them directly to the feeding formula.
teaching: Caregivers should use a written medication-through-tube plan rather than improvising crushing methods.
delegationScope: Medication administration must follow role, pharmacy guidance, and facility policy.
examTrap: Assuming any tablet can be crushed because the patient cannot swallow it.
oneLinePearl: Tube access does not cancel formulation safety.

title: Tube-Feeding GI Tolerance: Treat the Cause, Not Just the Stool
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Diarrhea, constipation, nausea, and distention during tube feeding have many causes—including medications, infection, rate, formula, hydration, immobility, and underlying disease. Do not reflexively blame the formula.
recognize: New antibiotics, laxatives, sorbitol-containing medications, infection, dehydration, or rapid feeding can alter stool pattern.
priorities: Assess the whole medication, infection, hydration, and feeding context.
Escalate severe distention, persistent vomiting, bloody stool, or signs of obstruction/sepsis.
assessMonitor: Track bowel pattern, abdominal exam findings, hydration, medications, feed rate, and infectious symptoms.
interventions: Implement ordered bowel or feeding adjustments based on cause.
medicationSafety: Do not add antidiarrheals or laxatives reflexively without evaluating cause and orders.
teaching: Report major changes in stool pattern or abdominal symptoms rather than repeatedly changing formula at home.
delegationScope: Routine stool documentation may be delegated; interpretation and escalation require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Changing formula before reviewing medications and infection risk.
oneLinePearl: Feeding intolerance is a differential diagnosis, not a formula diagnosis.

title: Home Feeding Pumps: Build a Failure Plan Before Failure
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Home enteral or parenteral feeding requires a backup plan for pump alarms, power loss, tubing problems, missed nutrition, and glucose-sensitive therapies. Training must include what not to troubleshoot independently.
recognize: Unexpected alarms, battery failure, occlusion, leaking tubing, or power loss can interrupt therapy.
priorities: Follow device-specific instructions and the clinical backup plan.
Escalate unresolved pump failure, line/tube damage, or symptoms of glucose/fluid instability.
assessMonitor: Review delivered volume, device function, hydration, glucose when indicated, and signs of device-site complications.
interventions: Keep emergency contacts and backup supplies accessible.
medicationSafety: Do not compensate for missed therapy by changing rates or insulin doses without instructions.
redFlags: Pump failure with no backup plan
teaching: Know the pump manual, support number, clinician contact, and emergency plan before leaving the care setting.
delegationScope: Home-care PN/LVN responsibilities depend on agency policy, state scope, and device competency.
examTrap: Speeding up later feeds to 'make up' a missed volume without an order.
oneLinePearl: Home technology is safest when failure is planned for in advance.
